title: Give a sensor's int[] buffer a List view

blocks.text: A vendor's sensor library samples a production line and writes each reading into an `int[]` buffer that you allocate and hand to it; it keeps writing into the same buffer for as long as the line runs. The analytics code takes a `List<Integer>`: it reads the latest samples, smooths outliers by writing corrected values back where the library will pick them up, and sorts or reverses the readings in place with `Collections`. Today the service copies the buffer into a new list every second, and the corrections never reach the library.

Finish `src/main/java/practice/IntArrayList.java`, a `List<Integer>` over the buffer: the constructor, `get`, `set` and `size`. `AbstractList` supplies the rest, and refuses `add` and `remove`, since the buffer can't grow. When you're done, the list and the buffer stay the same data in both directions, and every `java.util.Collections` algorithm that changes a list works on it. About six lines in total.

cases.says: the list holds the buffer's values, in order, and answers the usual List questions about them
the list has the buffer's fixed size, and a null buffer is refused at once
set through the list changes the value the list then reads
a sample the library writes into the buffer later shows through the list, and sorting the list sorts the buffer
set returns the value it replaced, which Collections.reverse and Collections.swap rely on

origin.section: Arrays.asList Adapts an Array Without Copying It, So Sorting the List Reorders the Array

concepts: Arrays.asList copies nothing: the list reads and writes the array, so sorting or setting through the list changes the array, and changes to the array show in the list.
Arrays.asList adapts arrays of objects only: given an int[] it returns a one-element List<int[]>, and the JDK has no List<Integer> view of an int[].
